source.title: Machine Learning Models that Remember Too Much
source.authors: Cong-Zheng Song; Thomas Ristenpart; V. Shmatikov

record.tranche_reason: The capacity-abuse experiments train models on synthetic inputs with labels encoding training-data secrets and report how well the models recover those labels; this bears conceptually on fitting arbitrary labels, though the experiments are malicious data augmentation rather than random labeling of the original training set.
record.gate_note: The paper reports capacity-abuse results on synthetic inputs with labels that do not correspond to input structure. It does not report a sweep over corrupted-label fractions, training-time comparisons, shuffled or Gaussian inputs, explicit-regularization ablations, or learning order. The cited Zhang et al. results are prior work and are not recorded as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study uses arbitrary-label memorization to construct a data-exfiltration attack. Its experiments evaluate deliberately added synthetic inputs with secret-encoding labels and the attack's performance, rather than completely random labeling of the training set under V1 or any other listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate for the capacity-abuse attack. The broader conclusion is that malicious training pipelines can encode and leak substantial training-data information while retaining useful accuracy and generalizability, including through black-box access.
record.recipe_differences: The study adds synthetic inputs with secret-encoding labels to the training data and uses a conventional training algorithm; it does not reproduce random labeling of the original training set.
record.method_sensitivity: Model size changes accuracy on the synthetic inputs: smaller CNNs decode less accurately than larger CNNs.

fits_no_version.finding: With 11K synthetic inputs added to LFW, smaller CNNs have substantially lower synthetic-input decoding accuracy than larger CNNs, while primary-task test accuracy is similar.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Capacity for deliberately encoding arbitrary secrets through synthetic training examples increases with CNN size while useful primary-task accuracy can be preserved.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS '17)
record.problems: For the result bearing on random-label fitting, exact synthetic-input accuracy is available only in a figure; the text describes the model-size trend but gives no values. The reported task uses secret-encoding labels and added synthetic data, not random labels on the original training set.
record.rows_left_out: Capacity-abuse tables report extraction quality and primary-task test accuracy across datasets, models, and synthetic-input counts (Tables 6 and 7). Those measures do not directly report the training accuracy on synthetic labels required by V1, so they are not cataloged as V1 rows. The exact synthetic-input accuracy values in Figure 4 are figure-only and not recoverable from the text.

untested.parts: Near-zero training error and chance test performance on a completely randomly labeled training set with unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Relative training time for true versus random labels and convergence as label corruption increases.
Zero training error on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily worsening test error across a random-label corruption sweep.
Whether conventional explicit regularizers prevent random-label fitting and whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
The order in which networks learn real-data patterns and memorize noisy labels.

record.verdict_notes: The near-100% fitting of randomized labels and features discussed in related work is attributed to Zhang et al., an original source, rather than established by this study. Attack reconstruction quality and primary-task accuracy do not establish the listed random-label claims.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses additional synthetic inputs with secret-encoding labels, not completely random labels on the original training set; it does not report chance test error on those inputs or compare unchanged training hyperparameters against the original random-label experiment.

rows.subject: CNNs with different number of filters in the last convolution layer (16, 32, 48, ..., 112)
rows.size_stated: different numbers of parameters; exact counts not stated
rows.operation_detail: Train on LFW with 11K malicious synthetic inputs in addition to the original data; evaluate accuracy on synthetic inputs.
rows.measure: Test accuracy on synthetic inputs (malicious-task decoding accuracy).
rows.locator: Figure 4 and section 6.7, Memorization capacity and model size
rows.note: Authors state smaller models have much lower synthetic-data accuracy than bigger models; no exact values are stated in the text.
rows.check: This measures the capacity-abuse attack on 11K deliberately synthesized inputs added to normally labeled LFW data. It does not measure V1's completely randomly labeled training set. Synthetic-input accuracy is accuracy on inputs used during training, despite the discussion calling it test accuracy. The supplied text gives only a qualitative model-size trend; Figure 4's numerical values are unavailable. The row also aggregates several model sizes.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
